utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. There are a couple of matters to raise before we start our business today. The first matter concerns the Prosecution motion to add certain documents to its 65 ter list, which also relates to the order of witnesses with respect to KDZ-88. So the Chamber is of the view that while the threshold for addition to the exhibit is certainly low, but given that we haven't received the translation of that document, we have a very minimal basis upon which we can draw any conclusions at the moment. So for that reason, the Chamber is of the view that it will not be able to decide the matter until it has reviewed the details of the diary itself. So in light of this situation -- yes, Mr. Tieger, do you have any observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Would it be helpful to the Court, and I don't know -- we've disclosed -- let me step back. We have disclosed, as I mentioned the other day, to the accused those portions of the exhibit that have been translated, and those are considerable. I also mentioned that with respect to the witness the Court just mentioned, the translations have been received and disclosed; that is, with respect to those portions that are relevant. So perhaps it would be of assistance to the Court, if it hasn't received those translations yet, to get those forthwith. So while the entirety of the exhibit has not been translated, considerable portions have, and as I mentioned, particularly those portions relevant to the upcoming witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered that submission from the Prosecution. However, the Chamber does not agree with you, Mr. Tieger, that your submission that would be okay to proceed with the KDZ-88 because the accused has the particular portions of the diaries that the Prosecution considers correspond to the witness. The thing may be that the accused needs to rely on other parts to ask further questions, and so I don't think it's realistic, in this situation, to call the witness before the recess. The Chamber is now requiring you to call him after the recess. As for the response from the accused, while the accused does not need to have undertaken an extensive analysis of the diaries in order to respond to its request for the addition to the Rule 65 ter list, but given the Chamber hasn't received any translation, so it will be appropriate for the accused to respond by the end of the first week, i.e., the Friday, 9th of July. So that's the first ruling of today. And the second matter relates to the scheduling, in particular tomorrow's hearing. Considering the accused has complained that he hasn't enough time to prepare for this witness, given the latest disclosure and given that he has spent about three hours and the remaining time for his cross-examination is about four hours, so if we sit until end of today, he will exhaust most of his time, so my suggestion is to sit three hours, just two sessions today, and leaving the remainder of the day for his preparation, and sit some time tomorrow morning. So it's up to the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. That is acceptable, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll sit two sessions, 9.00 until 12.30 today. That said, let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one small point of clarification. I'm not seeking to revisit the Court's ruling, but I wanted to make sure it wasn't predicated on any misunderstanding. When I spoke of the fact that the translations are complete and have been disclosed relevant to the upcoming witness, it doesn't mean simply those particular portions in which the witness maybe mentioned or reflecting meetings which he attended, but the entirety of the period during which he was present and about which he'll be testifying. I mean, there's a long, long period of time encompassed by those translations, running many, many months. So the portions of the diary that aren't translated represent -- excuse me. The portions of the exhibit that we're talking about now that aren't translated represent periods of time years later, for example, not the period of time in question. So I didn't -- to the extent there was a risk of any misunderstanding in that respect, I wanted to make sure that that was as clear as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it was clear, Mr. Tieger. The point I raised is that as a matter of practicality, the Chamber is unable to give its ruling until it has received and reviewed the translation of a document which is of 3.000 pages. And given that the completion of that translation will not be ready until the first week of July, or which is not clear at this moment, and I'm not sure whether the Chamber can make its ruling before the witness is coming, and that until that time, the Prosecution cannot rely on that document, i.e., until leave is granted to add to its list that document. So that was the crux of our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wonder if it wouldn't be possible to consider, Your Honour, the tendering, rather than the document in its entirety, those portions, the individual note-books relevant to the particular witness and that have been translated, which is another option, it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's a matter of a separate motion from yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. It may be if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If we could just have some clarity as to the identity of the next witness. There had been some question -- or we had a communication that another witness might be substituted ahead of Mr. Mandic, and we would like to know who to prepare for next. So if we could have some clarification of that, that would be helpful to us as we go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's news to me -- to us. We haven't heard about any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We received a letter last week to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In anticipation of the -- because of the uncertainties associated with the process we're engaged in now, we -- and in the interest of using our courtroom time as effectively as possible, we spoke with the Defence about the possibility of another witness in case there was a disruption in the schedule that wasn't anticipated. We are trying to obtain as much current information about next week's schedule as possible, and as I say, we've spoken with the Defence about that. We're looking for the most current update this morning, which we hope will resolve any uncertainties about next week's schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We had some certain matters -- administrative matters to deal with. So, Mr. Karadzic, let's start.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all. May I ask for 65 ter 30723 to be called up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for that, may I inform you, General, that this is an intercept of a conversation between Professor Koljevic and Miljenko Karisik, the chief of our Special Police Brigade. So it's the 30th of April, 1992. Professor Koljevic is calling from Lisbon. Please cast a glance at what he said. Can we please move on to page 2 in English. It's the same page in Serbian. Actually, sorry, I beg your pardon. You can see here that it's impossible to communicate by telephone between Sarajevo and Pale. Mr. Karisik is at Vraca. That is where the headquarters of the Serb MUP is, and he cannot reach Pale by telephone. Professor Koljevic is putting questions from Lisbon and providing certain instructions. Can we move on to page 2, please. Second page, please. At the top, you can see that, in English, that they cannot reach 783. That is the code for Pale. And this young men says that they are having problems too, that Pale seems to be cut off. And it was the Muslim side that had cut off Pale. You see here towards the bottom that they are discussing who it is who is actually shooting on the 30th of April. And as you can see, they are firing at the army at Zlatiste, and Koljevic is calling for restraint on our side. It had been agreed with Colm Doyle that European Community Monitors be positioned near all our artillery pieces so that they would be in a position to report who it was that was doing the shooting. You see here it says: "Yes, they shoot from Hum and Zlatiste." [In English] "They shoot from the direction of Sirokaca and Zlatiste." [Interpretation] Do you know that Sirokaca and Zlatiste are in the hills on the slopes of Mount Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you were to be observing fire from Zlatiste and Sirokaca that is falling on Serb neighbourhoods in town, would your conclusion be that it is Serbs that are firing at the Serbs in town?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated yesterday, I have a very limited knowledge of the geography of Sarajevo and these places. They mean absolutely nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you came here to testify. I am asking you the following: When shells fall on Sarajevo from the hills around Sarajevo, does it go without saying, as far as you're concerned, that it's the Serbs who are doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, yeah, on most occasions I would think that if shelling is coming from outside the city, it would be -- it would certainly be originating from Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, that is totally wrong. You know where Hum is? It is to the north of Sarajevo. We saw it here on a photograph. And Zlatiste and Sirokaca is to the south of Sarajevo, on the slopes of Trebevic, so they are firing from the hills, shells are falling on Sarajevo, and the Serbs are being blamed for it; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the witness has answered that question. As he clearly indicated, he has a very limited knowledge of the geography of Sarajevo. That's what we heard from the witness. Let's move on. I don't think there's any point of asking him about geography any further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, ethnic deployment and geography are two very important things, as far as -- where the shells are coming from and where they're falling. They are falling on Serb neighbourhoods, and yet the Serbs are being blamed for those shells. So why is this witness here? All right, I understand. Thank you. Can we have the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to what Koljevic is saying here: [In English] "We have made an arrangement with Doyle that he should bring those observers. Let them be taken where our artillery is and let that artillery be withdrawn. We cannot start the conference here without this done. This has been set as a condition." [Interpretation] Do you know that Muslims often put various conditions forth in order for the conference to continue, or, rather, that this showed that it was not in their interest to have the conference continue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't know which conference we're talking about. And any conference in April of 1992, I would have had limited knowledge or interest in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, as for the time when you were part of the conference, were the Muslims putting various obstacles in the path of the conference and various preconditions, and was it not obvious that it was not in their interest for the conference to continue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about 1993, yes, there were many occasions where each side participating in the negotiations placed preconditions on the continuation or some subsequent action being able to take place. But in all honesty, it was not just the Muslims who did this, but all of the parties involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, do you remember that all our positions were based on the unconditioned continuation of the conference? Give us one single example of a situation when the Serbs said, We are not going to go to the conference unless such and such a thing is done.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the present moment, I can't give you an example, Mr. Karadzic. But I can say that it is my general recollection that both sides or all sides participated and drove pretty hard bargains in the negotiating process, and from time to time refused to progress with the conference at all. Minor problems were sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, the Serbs did not do that. You're not going to find any such example, General; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, I can't give you a specific example right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to direct your attention to what Koljevic is saying. Well, that's what the document says: [In English] "Mobilisation cannot start until the artillery which is threatening the city is removed." [Interpretation] Further down, it says: [In English] "There should be no shells falling on the city anymore, and we cannot prove this came from Hum. You know that." [Interpretation] Then further down: [In English] "We can only take them there and tell them, 'These here are our artillery pieces.' "That is it. So I'd like to ask you to make sure that this is done, and let them go to some artillery positions. "Our positions." [Interpretation] So do you see that we are trying to bring the observers and monitors in to monitor our artillery pieces in order to be in a position to report that we are not the ones who are firing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly what this document says, but I have no knowledge of the tactical situation there. On the 30th of April, I, in fact, left the city to go to Jerusalem. This would seem to be a more appropriate question to be asking Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, we didn't have enough time for Mr. Doyle. But let me say this: It is clear from this conversation that the Muslims are firing from the hills on the north and the south, and that they are putting forth preconditions; namely, that the conference cannot continue until the Serbs stop firing, but it's actually the Muslims who are doing the shooting. Can I now have page 3, please. The next page in English, please. You see here that they are unable to reach Pale from Sarajevo. They cut them off. That means that it was the Muslims that cut off the telephone lines with Pale. And Koljevic says that it's very important that the white ones, that is to say, the monitors - they wore white suits - that they come to the spot and they see that we are not the ones who are shooting. Did you know anything about these ploys, that the Muslims were actually firing and accusing the Serbs of having fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any conversations amongst you, the representatives of the international community, if I can put it that way, that one had to exercise caution because different games are being played, and different tricks too?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I return to my evidence of yesterday that the events that were taking place in Sarajevo were not in the -- within the mandate of UNPROFOR and, quite rightly, belonged to the ECMM. And I believe that Mr. Doyle was one of the prominent leaders of the ECMM in Sarajevo. Once again, I can't talk about events that occurred when I was not there, and I certainly can't relate a written document to a tactical situation of which I've got no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, your statement is full of positions of this kind. You are referring to Sarajevo and other parts of Bosnia where you had never been. You easily resort to saying that it was the Serbs who were firing and that things like that were happening. We'll deal with that tomorrow. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the witness has confirmed any part of it. There's no basis on the part of the Chamber to admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, his entire statement shouldn't be admitted into evidence, Your Excellency. Then I suggest that all of that be taken out because it's useless. Can we have 0010 -- 01110 -- 1D01110? General, in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note in this document that the Karadzic translation is incomplete. And when comparing it against a CLSS translation, it seems to be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you mean that you have a CLSS translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, a CLSS translation exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we use it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But we would need to put it on ELMO. It's printing right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not in the e-court yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's not part of the Rule 65 ter exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have no objection to using the CLSS translation, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not, and I'm very thankful that it exists. But we, of course, can't translate the documents in their entirety, just the passages that are of interest to us, because we don't have the resources to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note it is a draft CLSS translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd be grateful if they could point out what it is that is wrong in our Serbian translation. Perhaps the Prosecution can point that out to us. And may we now have 1D01110 brought up, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we can have that Serbian version in e-court while we have the translation on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, General, do you agree that this is a daily report dealing with daily events that the minister of the interior is informing us about on the 2nd of May, 1992, Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that's what the document says. But I've not seen a previous example so I can't confirm that that's, in fact, you know, what you say it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 40 of your statement, you say that after your return, you were informed about the events that took place in your absence; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was briefed on them, yes; in particular, upon the ambushing of the JNA convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a report -- a daily report for the 2nd of May, 1992, so let's see what it says, what this report from the Ministry of the Interior and minister of the interior says. It says that "over the past 24 hours," or at 2430 hours, there was an unprovoked attack on the Serbs of Sarajevo by the Green Berets. Did you know of the existence of the Green Berets at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware the military forces of the Bosnian Presidency were called the Green Berets by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did those forces refer to themselves by that name?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that one of the main streets in Sarajevo is called the Green Berets Street?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, a witness said here that the Green Berets were something that the Serbs had imagined, it was a fantasy of the Serbs. Do you consider that to be true, too?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's have a look at what the minister is reporting on; that there was a perfidious attack by the Green Berets from the direction of Visoko at the villages of Vela and Zenik. Now, General, you mentioned Visoko. Do you remember passing by a Serbian checkpoint between Visoko and Ilijas in a village called Cakarcici [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Once again, I refer to my statement, that I had limited knowledge of the geography of Sarajevo. I'm aware broadly where Visoko is, though, but certainly not those villages mentioned in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the all-out attack with heavy weapons and snipers, so that means they attacked Vraca, the seat of the Serbian MUP. The attack lasted several hours, and hundreds of mortar shells were fired, damaging the buildings and several houses in Dobojska Street, some of which caught fire. And then again at around 1500 hours, there was a heavy artillery attack from infantry and sniper weapons, the same from the direction of Grbavica, Hrasno, and Pofalici neighbourhoods, and the Jajce Barracks. Do you know that the Jajce Barracks were up on a hill above Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know two barracks were on a hill overlooking Sarajevo. One which was formerly the headquarters of the 2nd Military District. I can't recall its name. And the other barracks was down closer to the Tito Barracks, and that was one of the barracks I was involved in evacuating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that there was a Jajce Barracks above Bascarsija up on the hill?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Karadzic, I have limited geographic knowledge of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you see here "Hrasno." That's at an elevation, and so is Pofalici and the Jajce Barracks. So if they're dropping from Hum, Zlatiste, Sirokaca, Jajce, Hrasno, and so on and so forth, do you understand, General, that they were all hills under Muslim control and that they were firing on Serb suburbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you that in the night between the 1st and 2nd of May, that is to say, before the killing of the security detail at the military hospital, that this attack took place on the Serbian MUP, and hundreds of mortar shells fell on our ministry building? Were you briefed about that or did that come under the general heading of the town was shelled?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter part of your answer. There was so much activity taking place at that time that a particular attack in one part of the city was reported basically as just part of the general calamity of what was occurring. Once again, I've got to say that UNPROFOR's footprint in the city was quite small. We had very limited capacity to investigate what was going on, and this was the responsibility of the ECMM. I would again point out to you that between the 30th of May -- or on the 30th of April and the 13th of May, I was not in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, let me ask you this now: If this were contained in a report, hundreds of mortar shells fell on the city, if it was that phrase that appeared, would you understand it that it was the Serbs doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not for the witness to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Likewise, there's no basis for us to admit this. The witness has confirmed nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have 1D01111. Four 1s, please, 01111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, this is another translation which we have a CLSS draft translation for. The difference between the Karadzic Defence translation and the CLSS translation, some nuances in words, but the difference being in the very first sentence, it simply lacks the words "last night's attack" -- the words "by members" are missing from the Karadzic Defence translation, and there's also three errors in relation to the names of the people that are listed. So if you wish to use the CLSS draft translation, we have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it could be put on ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With the understanding that the English translation will be replaced to this document. And one further question is: Are those translations the ones that have been pre-existing or the ones that have been newly translated by the CLSS?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Pre-existing, yes, Your Honour. The same for the last document and this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you found those pre-existing translated documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's put it on the ELMO. Let's hope it will be working again. General, in the meantime while we're waiting for that machine to be working again: One of the things we discussed in your absence, General, was the scheduling today. We'll sit until 12.30 today, and then we'll adjourn for today and we'll sit again tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just make the point that if Mr. Karadzic is going to read the translation, that he reads it correctly. He said a moment ago to the last document that hundreds of mortar shells were being fired. In fact, the translation says "a hundred." I mean, it's quibbling, but I would ask that he read the translation properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed with the B/C/S. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I said "a hundred."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is another daily report for the 3rd of May, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Why don't we give the English translation to the witness for his convenience. It will be easier for him to follow. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have our translation into English so that we can see what is wrong, what they say is wrong. So may we have our translation called up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed. [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you said yesterday that you believed that the Muslims had several mortars, 82-millimetre ones; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said that, it's perhaps a little inaccurate. I had a small quantity. I would think if they had 20 or 30, that would be the limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, do you claim that they didn't have any 120-millimetre ones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see -- now, I can't recall ever seeing a 120-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you believe their sources, that in Sarajevo, itself, they produced 80.000 shells for the 120-millimetre?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first time I've heard that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll bring the book in tomorrow, their source. Now, would you focus on the last paragraph, please. It says: "According to detailed information that is in the possession of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic of BiH, the victims of the 120-millimetre mortar attack carried out by the so-called TO BAH and other paramilitary formations against the area of Vraca-Sarajevo are as follows:" And then they listed several killed, the rest were injured. Do you know where Vraca is, General?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me help you out. Vraca is a hill above Grbavica. So Grbavica and Vraca are mostly inhabited by Serbs, and Vraca is almost a 100 per cent Serbian area. So do you see between the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1992, there was a heavy mortar attack, using 120-millimetre mortars, against this Serb settlement and that this many people were injured and killed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what this document says, but I was not in the city and I was not briefed on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in paragraph 40, you say that upon your return, you were briefed on the situation, and this is a drastic event. Did the ECMM give you the possibility of learning about this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I should take a moment to tell you exactly what happened when I returned to the city on the 13th of May. When I returned to the city on the 13th of May, I returned to the office for a short period of time and spoke with General MacKenzie. He, at that time, was preoccupied with the after-events of the evacuation of the first JNA Barracks, including the kidnapping of President Izetbegovic, so his briefing was necessarily broad and he hit the highlights. I also spoke with my UNMO headquarters staff, and they briefed me, in broad terms, what had happened in Sarajevo to the effect that there had been continued conflict, that there had been some fighting around the hill you call Hum, and then they briefed me on what my military observers had been doing in the UNPAs in Croatia. On the 14th of May, there was very heavy fighting, where nobody could leave their accommodation. On the 15th of May, when I was able to get into the headquarters, once again there was very limited staff there because the fighting was continuing. On the 16th and 17th of May, the headquarters left. So there was limited opportunity for people to be sitting down and briefing anybody in detail about events for which we had no operational responsibility. So I'd like to give you that rather lengthy explanation to explain why I've not got a detailed knowledge of what happened while I was away. It's pointless asking me about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let's look at a document before the 14th, just one. There are many of them, but we'll look at just one. But let me ask the Trial Chamber whether this can be admitted first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's a waste of time. General Wilson's clearly said he has limited knowledge. Unless you move on to relevant issues to which the general can give relevant answers, we'll find that you are wasting your time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I'll leave this document of the 6th of May and move on to a document of the 14th of May. 30753 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm sure you know Mrs. Plavsic, member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and vice-president of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telephone conversation between Mrs. Plavsic and Mico Stanisic, taking place on the 14th of May, 1992. Now, did you know that Mrs. Plavsic, right up until the 22nd of May, lived in Sarajevo, right up at the separation line?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We had cause to send some of our troops around to her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And most probably they had to drive her to your headquarters for negotiations; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On occasions. Also, she co-opted us once to attempt to evacuate her mother from the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Probably her mother or brother and sister-in-law. Anyway, take a look at this. Somewhere in the middle, Biljana Plavsic says: [In English] "Let me tell you fire must cease at 1400 hours sharp." [Interpretation] And then a little lower down: [In English] "Fire must cease at 1400 sharp. They too will. The Presidency too has decided that it should stop at 1400 hours so that we can go to UNPROFOR headquarter for negotiations." [Interpretation] And she's talking to somebody called Milos. And then the minister becomes included in the conversation. Mico Stanisic says: "Good afternoon, how are you," and so on. And we can see that Mrs. Plavsic even believes that she never actually met the minister, and says: "Have we ever met before," and so on. And then she says: [In English] "Mico, please, there should be negotiations at 1400 hours." [Interpretation] So they were probably the negotiations that you attended; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 14th of May, I was in my apartment and couldn't leave it because of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, we see what it says -- Biljana Plavsic says: [In English] "There is a five-day cease-fire there." [No interpretation]: [In English] "They were the first to open fire this morning."

utterances.speaker: MR. STANISIC
utterances.text: "They are still attacking here." So this exchange between the two -- : [In English] "This MacKenzie called me and said the Presidency had said they would cease fire at 1400 hours sharp, but we also have to cease-fire at ..." [Interpretation] And so on. Later on, Mico Stanisic: [In English] "But if there is an attack there as intensive as the one now is, people will have to defend themselves and everything else. Let them reduce the intensity of their attack. Just reduce the intensity and we'll stop immediately." [Interpretation] Do you see that the minister is asking them to reduce and says, We'll stop?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document says, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further down: [In English] "It will not be of you -- be us who cause a problem, but they have given their assurances before and still 100 soldiers got killed down there around the headquarter." [Interpretation] And so on. Therefore, General -- and I recommend this intercept to everybody to take a look. And on the 14th of May, early in the morning, you say in paragraph 41 that serious fighting, including widespread use of heavy weapons, broke out early in the morning and lasted all day. The hostilities certainly occurred in the immediate area of Dobrinja where "I was located in my apartment," et cetera, et cetera. Now, do you see that on that same day, the Muslims were attacking and that our people were asking for them to reduce that so that we could stop?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw on that day from my apartment, in fact, was the Serbs were attacking the immediate vicinity that I was in and that the very limited Presidency forces who were there, a ragtag group of young men with rifles, there by a policeman, they appeared to be mounting a rather unprofessional defence of the area. I can only say what I saw, Mr. Karadzic. But in the case of Dobrinja, where I was, when I was able to occasionally look out the window, the attacking was actually being done by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give us the time-frame again, General, when you saw that fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The time of the day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Morning, late morning, afternoon. Very heavy fighting. I spent most of the day, actually, in my bathroom, lying on the floor, because of the shrapnel and the rounds that were coming in -- into the apartment. But if I crawled out and looked out the window, which I did from time to time, I could see what was happening. And this attack went on most of the day, including a very heavy artillery attack which destroyed the Rainbow Hotel, which was the accommodation for the UN forces in UNPROFOR. It was a deliberate attack against that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how did you know who the Serbs were and who the Muslims were?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims were generally people running around in civilian clothes with rifles. The Serbs were the people in uniforms, with helmets, supported by tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh, I see. And you know -- knew which part was Serb and which part was Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: One side was attacking the other. By observation, I believe one group to be Serb, the other group to be Muslim. I was actually able to talk with the Presidency forces who were actually in the stairwell of my building. I chatted with them for half an hour to ask them what was going on. They told me that they were defending the area. They told me there were Presidency forces. I saw who was attacking them. They were Serbs in JNA-type uniforms. They were well organised. It was a good infantry attack, one that required training. I suspect it may have even been JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you mean to say that Mrs. Plavsic and the minister here are not telling the truth? It's not a press statement; it's a conversation that they weren't aware was being tapped.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation in this -- recorded in this intercept, Mr. Karadzic, is a sad commentary, really, on the many hundreds of cease-fires which were negotiated in the former Yugoslavia from 1991 through until at least the end of 1993, that I'm aware of, that were not respected by one side or the other. When the parties decided they seriously wanted to implement a cease-fire, they could do it. But for the most part, they didn't respect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you, General. What I'm asking you is this: Do you believe that these people are speaking sincerely here, a member of the Presidency calling up the minister of the interior, and they don't know each other, she can't remember whether they'd ever met, and they're saying what was taken on as the responsibility, to stop at 1400 hours? Is this a lie or is this authentic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's not for the witness to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you asked a member of the Green Berets or Patriotic League, you say, the Presidency forces, as you said -- or, rather, you asked them, but did you ask any Serb who was doing the attacking and who was on the defence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were firing at me, Mr. Karadzic. They were not looking for a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that the Serbs were firing on you and the Muslims weren't?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do mean to say that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself, General, to be a well-informed person and impartial person and an impartial observer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do consider myself sincerely to be impartial, as much as one can be. Everybody has prejudices, but in this case I tried very hard, as a professional, to be impartial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, of all these prejudices that you have, could you quote one that you have vis-a-vis the Serbs? Don't you see that you do have a prejudice against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can assure you, Mr. Karadzic, I don't have a prejudice against the Serbs. I have great sympathy for all the people of the former Yugoslavia. In my dealings with them, they're very nice people. Unfortunately, they were involved in bad politics, led by bad politicians.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please tender this into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The general knew nothing about this conversation, the content of this document. We will not admit this. Will you use it --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have 65 ter 30759. The general doesn't know anything about what the Defence is putting to him, and we will see, from other sources, that he actually claims to know so much. So can we now please have this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and some people from Nedzarici. Do you know where Nedzarici is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, so Nedzarici is really close to Dobrinja, just one street apart, so let us see what they say. I'm in Belgrade, as you can see from Ambassador Zimmerman's book, and I am calling the local Territorial Defence people from Belgrade to talk to them. So, General, do you see that Rade reports to me here? I'm asking him: "Can you tell me what is the situation down there?" He says: "Well, it's more or less okay. There's some shooting here at and at Mojmilo." And I'm asking: "Who's shooting?" And he says: "Well, they're shooting a little bit, they're responding, and we are doing that too." And then I say: "Okay, make sure that we are not shooting." And he says: "Okay. Should I relay that?" And I say: "Relay to everyone that it should be ceased." And he says: "Well, yes, I'm going to do that." And then I said: "You should call Biljana or somebody else before you start shooting so that she can inform UNPROFOR," and so on." So, General, were you aware of the fact that we always asked the Serbs to take fire for an hour or so and then to call UNPROFOR before responding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second before you answer, General. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. This intercept seems to be undated, so I don't know what date Mr. Karadzic is putting on -- when he was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It says "sometime in May."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a date, the 14th. We know that this is the 14th. It's your document, it's a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I understand it says "May," Your Honour, but it's unclear as to what date in May, both on the B/C/S transcript and on the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow your point. So, Ms. Sutherland, that the foundation of the question is somewhat incorrect, that's your position?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, it may or may not be that the witness is aware as opposed to what the date is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So with that caveat, let's hear what the general can answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer is that I was not aware that there had been a directive issued by the Serb authorities that Serb forces should suffer an hour's firing upon them before they took any action and reported to UNPROFOR. And, quite frankly, I think it's an unrealistic directive that anybody would subject their forces to this sort of action. I don't believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that before responding, we always informed UNPROFOR, telling them that we were forced to respond?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this was confirmed here by a UN observer. He said that we had always informed them before responding. A witness confirmed that here in court. And do you see down here, on page 2, Karadzic says: "Inform him that he should stop and that we do not fire before we are directly threatened"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's in page 2 in the Serbian version, at the bottom of page 2. Can we please have a look at that. Here you can see that I'm asking him to cease fire immediately, he should stop immediately. Can we please look at the next page in English? Well, yeah, it says here -- what line is it? [In English] "Tell him to stop, and we are not shooting until we are under an extreme threat." [Interpretation] Does that mean that we should take -- that they should take fire for as long as they can and only then respond?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got no idea what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General, you're a soldier. Until we are under extreme threat, the kind of fire that causes casualties, and that we should respond only when we start taking casualties. This is what it means, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a politician said to me that as a soldier, then I would politely try and disagree and ignore it anyway. And I'm sure you must have had difficulty with your own generals if they were the sort of directives they were issuing. It's quite unrealistic to expect soldiers in combat to lie down and take fire upon themselves meekly until they start taking casualties. As a broad response, it's very unrealistic. Nobody is going to do that, Mr. Karadzic. I'm sure your generals would have told you that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I agree that I often made unrealistic demands to our officers and that we often clashed. So I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The general knew nothing about this, Mr. Karadzic. Ask some questions which the general can answer. Now move on to really relevant questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General, was there a way for you to see who started the fight and who was firing from what side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what time-frame, please, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the time-frame is your stay there, the 13th of May until the 24th of June.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our standard operating procedure as military observers was that you only verified information that you actually observed yourself. If you received reports about something that happened, you had to somehow or other support that with evidence from another source. And even when you did that, you reported the fact that you had not seen it, so you couldn't confirm it, but it was based on reports from X or Y. So the short answer to your question is: In May of 1992, in Sarajevo, we had a very limited footprint on the ground. A lot of the information coming to us was from your liaison officer actually located in the PTT, and similarly from the Presidency forces. We only ventured out into the city when we had actual missions to do. It was not a place to touristically drive around, enjoying yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Should I take it, then, that once the fighting started, you had no way of knowing who actually started the fight?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very true. We had to listen to what both sides said and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- inevitably each side would say, We didn't start it; the other side did. That was the standard reply in the former Yugoslavia about almost every incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that General Mladic made efforts to prevent casualties among innocent people, including young soldiers, and that he issued instructions to that effect to his people in the field, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. Quite to the contrary, he seemed to take a lot of actions that resulted in the death of a lot of people, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what appeared to you is why we have such problems, because your impressions are presented here as evidence, and it's not evidence. Could we please look at 65 ter 30793.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No speech, Mr. Karadzic. Ask your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at this document. This is the well-known intercept of Mladic's conversation with an unidentified male on the ground. The date is the 25th of May, 1992. And, well, here we have the document. He says: "What is going on in Sarajevo?" And he is warning them that they should be persistent in observation, that observers should be posted, that they should be well rested, and the moment the first bullet is fired at Jusuf Dzonlic Barracks or "Marsal Tito" Barracks, and if a single soldier is wounded either at the front or in the barracks, "I will retaliate against the town." So what you said a little while ago, that a general will not take fire, but will respond. Can we please look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, while we're waiting for page 2 to appear: Did you take Mladic's words as his intention to retaliate against civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I spoke to him on the 25th of May at a meeting I had with him and Mrs. Plavsic, he said if the barracks were not evacuated within three days, he would level the city. The city had a lot of civilians in it. If he's going to level the city, he's going to cause a lot of civilian casualties. That's exactly what I understood his threat was. As it turned out, he carried out that threat. On the night of the 28th of May, three days later, the barracks had not been evacuated. He unleashed on the city a most horrendous attack which he personally directed. Now, he issued this warning in the presence of Mrs. Plavsic. She didn't contradict anything he said. I assume the position that General Mladic gave to me was that of General Mladic and the political leadership of the Bosnian Serbs. I took it very seriously. I reported back to General Nambiar this conversation, and I passed it on to the Presidency as a warning, as requested by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you say, yourself, that General Mladic is asking for this to be relayed to the Presidency. Does he want to fire on the city or does he actually want to avoid having to do that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wants the barracks evacuated. And if the barracks aren't evacuated within three days -- I'm talking about the meeting on the 25th of May, not this document. If the barracks are not evacuated, he's going to attack the city. He's going to level the city, as he puts it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you: Did Mladic wish to fire or did he wish not to fire? Did he ask you to relay his warning to the Presidency precisely in order to avoid having to shoot at them; yes or no? Did he ask you to relay to the Presidency this warning of his?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speculate what motivated General Mladic, but I can say that I did pass the message to the Presidency, as requested by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come that you don't know what drove General Mladic, after the 2nd and the 3rd and the 15th of May in Sarajevo and in Tuzla respectively? The butchery of the soldiers as they were pulling out, was this reason enough for a general? Would you, yourself, say, well, this should not be repeated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on what motivates General Mladic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And would you -- after three massacres, would you have warned the Presidency not to let that happen again? Would you, as a general, try to protect your troops by warning the Presidency that this should not happen again?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really put myself in General Mladic's position, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, put yourself in your position. If you had three massacres after assurances were made for a safe withdrawal, what would you say to the Presidency if you had two more barracks that had to be evacuated? Would you have warned them or would you have pussy-footed with them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is not required -- the witness isn't required to speculate, Mr. Karadzic. Move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 3 of this document so that we can see what Mladic says to this guy who is in the field. It's page 3 in the English version and page 2 in the Serbian version. We're on the right page in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can see in the English: [In English] "You can endure more than they can." [Interpretation] So he's encouraging this man who is in the blockaded barracks, the Jusuf Dzonlic and the "Marsal Tito" Barracks, the people there are encircled, and he's encouraging this man, telling him, You can endure much more than they can. And then he goes on to say: "I don't want to kill the people. I don't want to destroy the city. I don't want the innocents to suffer. Those who want to fight, let them remain in Sarajevo. Let them allow the army to pull out. Let them pull out the civilians. And if they want to fight, we will fight. It's better to fight somewhere in the hills than in the city." Is this more than clear indication that Mladic wants to avoid firing on the city, itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document says. But on the same day, I met General Mladic, and he made it quite clear to me that it was his clear intent to attack the city if the barracks were not evacuated. I took his threat very seriously, to the extent that I formally reported it to my superior in General Nambiar. Words are cheap, Mr. Karadzic. It's what you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you see where he says here: "The people have to live somewhere. We do not want to fight." Do you see that in this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General, if you have to relay a message to the Presidency, do you feel it is realistic to relay a harsh message or a mild message, in light of the three massacres that had already happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I relayed the message that General Mladic asked me to relay, and that is that if the barracks were not evacuated within three days, he would level the city. That's the message I relayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you agree that when you send a message of this sort, it needs to be harsh, harsher than -- well, far harsher than what you actually mean? We see a difference between what he's telling his soldier on the ground and what he tells you. He says to those people on the ground, Peace, and he is telling you that there would be retaliation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me to speculate on the intent of his conversation with his men in the barracks. Clearly, these people are under great pressure, and he's trying to raise their morale, saying, It will be all right, I'll look after you. That's what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. But you do admit that he is telling this man who is on the ground that he doesn't want to fire on the city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document says, Mr. Karadzic. I again say --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is already included in the associated exhibit of this witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- and it was marked for identification as Exhibit P1041.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please look at 30824, 65 ter 30824, please. And I would like to ask the Registrar to check whether this has been admitted already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Mr. Baros is? He was a colonel and perhaps even a general.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mention him in your reports. He participated in the talks regarding the withdrawal from the "Marsal Tito" Barracks.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought his name was Bebeska [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, how did -- how was the Jusuf Dzonlic Barracks evacuated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Which barracks, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Jusuf Dzonlic. It was evacuated before the "Marsal Tito" Barracks.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's the one I think it is, it was a very small barracks containing only a small number of troops high up on a hill; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally attended the evacuation of that barracks. It was done by vehicles. The vehicles were pre-loaded by the occupants of the barracks, and some UN vehicles, which I was a passenger in one, escorted them safely out of the city. There was some minor problem leaving the barracks, where the crowd wanted to pull one of the drivers out of the cabin and do whatever with him then, but I interceded [Realtime transcript read in error "was seated"] and we were able to leave safely. It was quite a well-conducted operation, I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be Viktor Bubanj. But Jusuf Dzonlic came under heavy attack, and you mentioned it yesterday, because the column took a turn somewhere?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- I thought that was after "Marsal Tito" Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at this intercept, sir. So he first speaks with Potpara, and Potpara reports to him that everything is quiet, so Mladic wants to know what the situation is like in the barracks. And he says it's quiet, and he says: "Be extremely cautious." And then he says: "They want to provoke us into firing on the city by attacking the barracks." And then if we move on to the next page in the English language: "Tell the people so that they are aware of it." That's what Mladic says: "Be very cautious," Mladic says. And then in the end, he talks to Baros. He says: "Is this Baros?" We need the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Sorry, Dr. Karadzic. Just to note a mistake in the transcript. It's at 38.5. The general said that he interceded, and it's been transposed as "I was seated." It doesn't make any sense. He's talking about where he interceded with the crowd that was trying to pull the driver out of the car. It needs correcting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you can see that he now gets Baros on the line, and a little bit further down Mladic says: [In English] "You have heart problems? You'd better take some more rest." [Interpretation] And then he wants to know whether this is Baros, and then we follow their conversation. Baros was the commander of the "Marsal Tito" Barracks, was he not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You note that he attended a meeting, but let us move on. Could we please have the next page both in English and in Serbian. The next page in English: [In English] "Get ready. Do not let them humiliate you, as they did with Jusuf Dzonlic Barracks." [Interpretation] Further down: [In English] "We left all the heavy weapons for them there, and despite of that, they attacked the column and they would massacre all of you. Don't worry, all of you will get out. Just hang on there, there will be no problem." [Interpretation] So the column from the Jusuf Dzonlic Barracks had come under attack despite the fact that all the heavy weapons had been left there. Did you know that all the heavy weapons had been left behind in all the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the agreement that was negotiated with the Presidency. Yes, I'm aware that that was one of the conditions of the evacuation of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In this intercept they say those who have peace will have it. There was a mass attack on the next page. I recommend that all the parties should read it. Thank you very much. I would like to tender this into evidence. It speaks about the events that the general here had participated in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has been marked as MFI D207.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at the next page in English. I would just like to go through one more thing, one passage, one response by Mladic. We should go one page further down in English. The next page, the next page in English. Well, it seems that we need the next page again in the English language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see what he says here: "I share the same opinion. We think in the same way. If they want peace, they will have it. I ordered, as soon as I came last night ... it was an all-out attack against the units and you. There was shooting, and somehow I managed to calm down the people here, to put everything under control, to stop the fire. As for what they are producing now, they probably have pantomime performers, some good imitators who are able to imitate our voices properly. I mean your voice, my voice, and anyone's voice." So on the 29th, he's -- Mladic is telling his officer that on the 28th somebody broadcast a recording of his voice, and he claims it is an imitator. So he goes on to say they are making a circus of it and they are deluding their people and it is not true that they gave such orders. Did you know that Mladic made this claim, that the Muslims are, among other things, imitating his voice?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And here he goes on to say: "Pass this information on to every single soldier. Do not mess around in any circumstances. Do not risk your lives, because nobody has a life in reserve. We will not shell the town unless they violate the agreement, unless they put you in danger. But have you to be very careful. Do not trust them even one bit." So General Mladic is talking to his people on the ground in peaceful terms, and he wants you to relay a very harsh message to the Presidency. Do you see this as a logical behaviour on the part of an officer whose soldiers are at risk?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: What -- can I ask what date this intercept is, please, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember 29th of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 29th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, I can read what it says here. I didn't participate in this conversation. But the denial here of Radovan Karadzic -- or of General Mladic is surprising, because when the tape was played, it was played in Serbo-Croat, and two JNA officers independently said it was Mladic directing the fire of artillery. It was a tape produced by the Presidency forces, but two JNA officers said that that was Mladic. So I don't know why he's saying this to the troops in his barracks. In short, it's a lie, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Mladic say that publicly or is that what he's telling his people on the ground? He didn't say it to the media. That's what he said to his own people so that they would know the truth. Why would he lie to his own people? Did you ever see Mladic saying that in public, that his voice was being imitated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's right, because he never said that in public. If he said that for the media, then you could have had that kind of suspicion. However, do you know that Mladic had clashed with these two JNA officers because they had brought rifles to the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that General Mladic's position on the evacuation of the barracks is that no weapons should be handed over. The reality is that it was General Panic, General Mladic's superior officer, who ordered him in the end to get on with the job and hand over the weapons. Mladic said to me, quite clearly and firmly, that I should clearly understand that it was not him handing over the weapons, it was the JNA. He didn't want to be associated with the act of handing over the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll have a break. But before that, did you say that General Mladic was talking to his people in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Mladic, on two occasions, that is to say, this one and the previous one, he was talking to people who were encircled. They were JNA, but Mladic was no longer JNA after the 20th of May, that is, so that is to say a week before this. He is giving them encouragement, and he considers it to be his duty to help them be evacuated without a massacre. We cannot understand Mladic without looking at the context. He is -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And these two generals, do you agree that they had clashed with Mladic and that at that point of time they were not Mladic's superiors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which two generals, please, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, all right. You remember Boskovic? Boskovic brought 6.000 rifles, and Mladic is distancing himself from that; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Mladic subordinated to Panic at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe firmly so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about this document? Oh, oh, it's been admitted already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to update the Court on the status of some developments in the witness scheduling issue, some of which were alluded to earlier today. First, we did notify -- oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. And we need to move into private session to address those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. President, we haven't provided the time estimate for this witness yet, and we'll do that by e-mail within -- by the end of the day today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope that will be a reasonable one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we get someone who really knows what it was that was going on in Sarajevo, then we are going to require time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, could you please have a look at paragraph 61, or perhaps you can remember without even looking at it. It speaks of the shelling of the bread line, and you say: [In English] "Another attack on civilians, admittedly a horrendous one, and I assumed the Serbs to be responsible. I presumed this because attack on civilians by the Serbs were occurring at that stage on an almost daily basis." [Interpretation] Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written, yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then have a look at paragraph 62. You are talking to General Mladic, and Mladic is telling you that: [In English] "Mladic, he stated that the Serbs had not been responsible for the bread line attack and that the Presidency had perpetrated this incident -- the incident. His body language was such that I attributed some credence to his statement. Radovan Karadzic and Biljana Plavsic were also part of this conversation and also denied the Serb responsibility -- that Serbs were responsible." [Interpretation] On what day did you talk to Mladic and me and Biljana?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was during the airport negotiations which started on or about the 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at 63 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I was advised -- I was advised there has been no French translation for one of my colleagues. I haven't heard any French. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I repeat something? No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at paragraph 63, then, where you say: [In English] "A technical investigation was conducted by French soldiers at the site of the shelling after the arrival of General MacKenzie in Sarajevo. I believe that the investigation involved crater analysis. The result of the investigations were inconclusive, in that whilst a round could have come from a Serb position, there were also Muslim positions in the range of fire, and therefore firing from one of those positions could not be ruled out." [Interpretation] Why, then, did you decide to say that it was the Serbs after all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't believe I ever said it was the Serbs. I said the conclusion that is meant to be drawn from those paragraphs is there is doubt about that particular incident, as to who perpetrated the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in paragraph 61, you say: "And I assumed the Serbs to be responsible ."

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had at the time of the attack assumed that. But when the investigation was subsequently conducted sometime after the 11th of June, that corrected my assumption. I'm saying here that there's some doubt, that it could not be conclusively said that the Serbs carried out that attack. I don't know who carried out that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if you do not know, you decide that it's the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the attack first took place, because it was such a regular event at that time, I assumed, incorrectly perhaps, that it was the Serbs. Subsequent investigation threw some doubt upon that assumption. I'm certainly owning up to that, and I guess if you are demonstrating that I do have impartial views about what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, there is no presumption of innocence for the Serbs; right? The Serbs are innocent only if it is proven to be the case that it was the Muslims who had done something; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you, General, that not a single one of these well-known incidents that involved massive casualties was not committed by the Serbs and that we have evidence to support that, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speculate on that, Mr. Karadzic, without the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Actually, we have to move into private session briefly. D230, please, could I have that in e-court. Private session briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We're still in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have 01072. That's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the meantime: Why did you not discuss that incident with Mr. Izetbegovic and you did discuss it with us, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I discussed that incident with the Serb side because I was attending other meetings with you at that time. In terms of the Presidency, it may well have been raised by them when Mr. Thornberry and I visited them for negotiations in the period after the 2nd of June. My recollection is broadly that they would have protested and highlighted this attack. It was -- even in Sarajevo at the time, with limited media people present, it was given great coverage around the city and played on the television for hours on end, just kept repeating the same images. So it was quite well known within the city and I'm sure would have been discussed with both sides. As I said earlier, I've included this incident in my statement simply to illustrate the fact that all -- that there was no clear good guys and bad guys in the events in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you know that the media were at the site of the explosion beforehand? That was broadcast all over the place, that they were ready?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that allegation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
