utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall, General, that I had asked for the demilitarisation of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that you'd asked for that on a number of occasions. The first time you asked for that I can't put a date on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree and do you recall that I had said that the Serb neighbourhoods in Sarajevo were attacked every night by the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall a specific incident, but I believe it's highly likely that you did raise that on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember why the United Nations did not succeed in carrying out a demilitarisation, why? Who was it that prevented that from taking place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it was both sides, Mr. Karadzic. In the context of the opening of the Sarajevo Airport, it was suggested by the United Nations that weapons be withdrawn from around the airport and also from 30 kilometres from the city, which was a measure which was vigorously opposed by you and your military adviser. That's part of the demilitarisation process, that you had a very strong position on that you would not accept. My recollection is that you wanted the city to be passed to the control of the UN with a green line drawn somewhere in the city which would segregate Serb areas from other ethnic areas of the city. I don't believe a map was ever produced during those negotiations, nor was there a discussion of any suburbs. Your basic position during those negotiations was that you were not prepared to take the first step in demilitarisation, which would have been the withdrawal of heavy weapons from the vicinity of Sarajevo. It was the Serb position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember, General, that we had more weapons and they had more infantry? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that's true. Certainly, you had more heavy weapons. I don't know with any accuracy what the relative infantry strengths were. I wouldn't be surprised if there was a marginal majority in favour of the Presidency forces of infantry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The translation of -- or the court report does not reflect what Mr. Karadzic asked to the witness. As I remember, his question is that the Serbs had more weapons, while the other side had more infantry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I was just going to intervene. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we agree that the Serbs had more weapons, and I say that the Muslims had more infantry. Do you remember me saying that that strikes a strategic balance?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if I tell you now that it does strike a strategic balance, would you, as a general, accept doing away with your element of strategic balance and the other side not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a board game, Mr. Karadzic. That's -- what we're talking about here is perhaps tactical balance rather than strategic balance. It depends very much upon the circumstances. Some elements of military power are employable in some situations and not in others. For example, fighting in an urban area is best done by infantry. Fighting in open country is best done by armour. Employment of heavy weapons in an urban context is very difficult because of the collateral damage. You cannot simply say left and right, therefore there's balance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, do you know that even a partial acceptance of measures on the part of only one side would give the other side the advantage; yes or no? Just give us a yes-or-no answer. Would -- if the Serb weapons were done away with, would it give the advantage to the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what measures you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if the Serbs were to remove, and there are three times less of them, three times less infantry, if they were to remove the heavy weapons and the Muslims were to do nothing at all, would that give the opposite side the advantage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you take a look at paragraph 3. Read out paragraph 3, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mr. Karadzic referred first in general to the situation of the Serbs in Sarajevo who are in control of areas in the suburbs and parts of the city and who are attacked practically every night by the Green Berets. He indicated the Serb forces are inexperienced and self-organised. That Mladic does not have all under his command, but that they are trying to bring them under control. He added that because of the their inexperience, they overreacted to attacks. He indicated that they were willing to remove artillery from the hills if attacks on the suburbs stopped." This document, I assume, is, because you have not introduced it, is a report of General Morillon's discussions the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was -- this is Exhibit P1036. It came in as an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, as a soldier, how long would you need -- how much time would you need from the Territorial Defence and organised groups to turn those into an efficacious army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's impossible to speculate. I mean, I don't know the details of armaments levels, of training, deployment, what the operational expectations are. Mr. Karadzic, it's impossible to give an accurate answer to that. It would take some length of time, depending on how complex the problems were. It takes about two years to produce a reasonably good soldier of intense training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to paragraph 4 now. May I ask you to read it out, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary. We have it before us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's all read it, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say there that: "Karadzic went on to say that they," the Serbs, "would like to demilitarise Sarajevo, under United Nations supervision, with only police forces to remain to maintain law and order, Serb police in Serbian-controlled parts and Muslim police in Muslim areas"? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why was that not accepted? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a very good idea, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Will you tell it to us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of our experience in the Croatian UN-protected areas, where the military forces who were fighting there, when it came time for them to withdraw under the agreements accepted by all parties, these military groups suddenly turned into policemen. So what had happened, an army had been converted into a police force. In effect, there was no demilitarisation of the UNPAs, other than the concentration of heavy weapons. So the UN, with that experience so recently found in Croatia, would be very suspicious of any suggestion that this should be repeated again in another situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know what the Muslim motive was to oppose the demilitarisation of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speculate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that the first motive -- the prime motive was to gain control of the whole city and the second motive was Sarajevo was an important joker or trump card in gaining international sympathies and international military intervention, would that sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speculate on that, Mr. Karadzic. I don't know what motivated their actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is the Muslim side aware of what Karadzic proposed in negotiations with Nambiar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would have been made aware of that when Mr. Thornberry arrived in Sarajevo on the 2nd of June, several days after this meeting here, and proceeded to negotiate the opening of the airport. This would have been one of the matters discussed with both sides, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But as a military man, as a soldier, can you tell us whether Sarajevo would have been calmer, even on the assumption, for example, that somebody were to change clothes into a police force, if what Karadzic proposed had actually been acted upon?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may well have been calmer, but would not necessarily have changed the actual security situation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph 6 there, where he says: [In English] "He felt that the Bosnian Serbs were in a no-win situation to be blamed or to be defeated." [Interpretation] They were in a no-win situation. And then lower down, paragraph 7, General Morillon asks whether we can-- [In English] "And it would be their interest to show their goodwill by stopping it, by stopping shelling. He asked Karadzic whether he was in a position to do so." [Interpretation] Number 8 says: [In English] "Karadzic replied in the affirmative. Mr. Koljevic qualified this by saying that they thought they could persuade the people on the ground to stop the shelling." [Interpretation] Doesn't that tell you that it was still a question of self-organised groups?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I acknowledged in my statement, Mr. Karadzic, that at the very beginning of the conflict, that I understood that there were groups who were not necessarily fully under control of General Mladic, and I accepted the fact that it was taking him some time to get control of them. But that does not include artillery resources. We're talking here about village militias. He would have had, my belief, a very firm control over heavy weapons and their firing into the city. These were weapons that were passed to him by the JNA. And, indeed, by the 30th of May, in my assessment, were still being fired by the JNA, because they would not have left behind their troops in the barracks. The JNA would not have fully withdrawn until all of their troops were out of the barracks. Also, my observations later in May were that the nature of the fighting was being carried out by highly competent military people who I also suspect were remaining JNA people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, those are all assumptions, General, sir. We heard from another witness here, also a soldier, that there was a shortage of capable officer cadres and especially specialists in weapons, and so on, marksmen and so on. Now, do you say that the Territorial Defence did not have access to heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the territorial force had access to. I'm simply saying that heavy weapons would have been a very high priority for General Mladic to gain and remain control of -- in control of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I put it to you, General, and I tell you that we have heard evidence here whereby a territorial unit took from a company from their Territorial Defence stock even Howitzers. Now, do you know how the system of the Territorial Defence functioned and the system of total national defence and social self-protection in Yugoslavia, for example; do you know how that worked?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Broadly I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know the doctrine, as it was called, of an armed people? Have you heard of that doctrine?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not heard of that specific description.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that the Territorial Defence existed -- a unit of the Territorial Defence existed in every enterprise, every company, and that they had their weapons depots and commands, and everybody was duty-bound to defend his country once it was threatened, once it was in danger, does that sound something that you are familiar with and had heard about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that, and I believe that to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the Territorial Defence had access to heavy weaponry as well. And, as you say, the village -- how did you put it -- village paramilitary groups, that was the territory Defence of each and every village, each local commune. They had access to light and heavy weapons alike. Do you accept that now if I tell you that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. If you say that to be true, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we take a look at the next page of this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 14: [In English] "If and when we get confirmation from Mr. Karadzic that he will be able to deliver on stopping the bombardment, we will get in touch with President Izetbegovic to proceed with the other aspects." [No interpretation]: [In English] "... just been advised by Karadzic's assistant that they could not make Sarajevo because of weather, but by phone Mladic had indicated that bombardment would stop. We will see how things are ..." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. That was paragraph 15. So what Mladic controlled, that would cease. And from the previous paragraph, we see Koljevic saying that, We'll try and convince people on the ground not to shoot. Do you know, General, that, for example, in Nedzarici, a purely Serbian settlement, it was attacked on a daily basis and that nobody had the right to tell them, Stop shooting, don't shoot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't surprise me that Nedzarici was attacked on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This document has already been admitted, it's an exhibit, so we can move on. May we have 65 ter 01078 called up next. It is possible that that is also an exhibit under a P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Exhibit P1039.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you attend this meeting, General, on the 3rd of June at the airport in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It wasn't at the airport at Sarajevo. It was held, actually, in Lukavica Barracks, but it was about the airport. That's why the subject reads that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I apologise. You're quite right. May we now have the next page displayed. Or just a moment, let's stay with page 1. Can we go back to page 1: [In English] "The basic issue, of course, remains who will politically control the airport which would be under UN control. The answer of the Serbs is that they will. We have suggested that they think again." [Interpretation] Now, on the next page, paragraph 2, the Presidency stressed the urgency. Do you see paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this man, Mr. Somun, was a little more extreme than we believed at first; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by that question. I didn't have a view whether he was extreme, or moderate, or conservative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]: [In English] "We said that the suffering of the people had become a worldwide scandal and that so far as we knew, there was no prospect of it being solved by magic or external military intervention." [Interpretation] What made you mention military intervention there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think following the bread line attack of the 27th of May, there had been extensive coverage in the international community, and there was some discussion in the international community that military intervention was an option. And I can't say it with certainty, but I suspect that this had been passed to the Serb leadership in some of their various negotiations. And certainly I believe it was a hope, I would say, of the Presidency at that time that there would be an intervention, and it was one of the considerations that they had to take into account in their negotiations and in developing a strategy and a policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So may we conclude that the Presidency, as you call it, although it was the Muslim government because we were the Presidency too, Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic being members of the Presidency, that the Muslim government -- it didn't suit the Muslim government for things to run smoothly, because if things ran smoothly following Serb proposals, there would be no intervention; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the United Nations confirmed that the Muslims hampered the taking over of the airport. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, may we turn to page 3, please. Paragraph 4: [In English] "Izetbegovic showed us the destruction brought on the Presidency, shelled most nights. (It does not seem to have a single piece of glass left undamaged). He ended by saying that he did not believe there could be an agreement; the reopening of the airport could come about only by foreign military intervention." [Interpretation] Do you see that he would welcome military intervention and that, therefore, it was logical that he would make it difficult for a take-over of the airport?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This cable, drafted by Mr. Thornberry, signed by me, and going up our chain of command, is a record of the negotiating positions of the two parties, and you'll be aware, Mr. Karadzic, that in negotiations people adopt and abandon various negotiating positions during that process. This is a record of the first day of negotiations, so it's defining, if you wish, the opening positions. What is stated in this cable and the reality can be quite different. The airport was opened. Both sides did agree to it in the end. In regards to the first part of your question, I'm sure the Presidency would have welcomed a foreign intervention. It would have certainly assisted their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have every respect for your understanding of negotiating tactics whereby extremist views are put on the table straight away and then that they relent later on, but why do you take that -- do you not take that into account when Mladic is giving a message, that it is an extremist one, but in reality different?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My experience with General Mladic was that he generally carried out his threats, he generally did what he said he would do. Therefore, I gave serious consideration to what he was saying and believed him, he would carry out his threat. And as it turned out, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it didn't turn out that that's what he did, General. But, of course, he tried to be convincing. Otherwise, you would have seen through it and there would have been no result. But can we have 65 ter 01555 next, please. Possibly that is a P number and a Prosecution exhibit too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P1045.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the following day, discussions -- airport talks of the 4th of June. Did you attend that meeting, General?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we can look through the whole document, but let's focus on paragraph 2 now. Let's see what Karadzic says there: [In English] "The afternoon began with us summarising to them some ideas on an airport regime. Karadzic interrupted at one point to say that this was a Muslim position, and all argued that the withdrawal of heavy weapons would tilt the balance in Sarajevo to the Muslim side to such an extent that Serbs would be butchered or have to flee." [Interpretation] Do you see, General, that our position was quite clear; with the removal of the only Serb advantage would lead to our catastrophe?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, we quite clearly understood the Serb position in this regard and the reason for that, and that's why the regime that was proposed actually left the Serb artillery in position, within range of the airport, but monitored by UN observers, who would report if those weapons engaged the airport. That was the regime. It left your weapons and your tactical advantage in place, but enabled the airport to be opened with some confidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you agree that the only reason -- our only reason not to remove the weapons around Sarajevo was precisely this fear of a massacre or the expulsion of Serbs from the places they lived in, or, rather, a disruption of the balance?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speculate on what motivated your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at number 3 now. Karadzic, somewhat in the middle, and Plavsic, on the somewhat less ideological, somewhat more humanitarian wing -- that was paragraph 2. And now number 3: [In English] "They explained that Karadzic's position in Lisbon had been taken in the context of the UN taking over supervision of the whole city; i.e., superintending a green line between two communities, each with its own police. Only in such context of physical disengagement, they said, did withdrawal of heavy weaponry to a distance from Sarajevo make sense." [Interpretation] So why, in your opinion, was the whole of Sarajevo not demilitarised? You referred to the zones, but here there would be complete management and control by the UN over Sarajevo, and do you remember that I proposed that Sarajevo would be declared an open city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that, Mr. Karadzic, but there are a number of proposals contained in this. The proposal that there be a green line created with police forces, as you call them, maintaining security there was not acceptable to the Presidency. It was not acceptable under any circumstances. Another element of a demilitarisation, that is, the withdrawal of heavy weapons, was not acceptable to you. The whole proposal at that time was not worth pursuing. Neither side would give it serious consideration. What our focus was was opening the airport and proposing to you and to the Presidency a regime that was acceptable to both sides.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now move two pages forward, please, the third page from this one. It should be our 063971, just one more page. The next page in the English language, please. So number 1: [In English] "The proposed demilitarisation elements of the plan leave the Serbian people in the area of Sarajevo vulnerable to the B-H forces and might cause the flight of thousands of Serbs from this area."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So these are the key points in the Serb response. And number 3 says: [In English] "The concept of demilitarising the area will be accepted only if the entire city is demilitarised and police forces from both sides secure the areas beyond the fire lines." [Interpretation] And then on the next page, the Serb alternative plan: [In English] "They propose the following alternative plan: "The sides should announce and honour a cease-fire in Sarajevo and stop all combat activities in the area, including certain corridors." [Interpretation] General, sir, what more could we have done without destroying the Serb community in Sarajevo? We proposed actively and accepted other people's proposals if they were consistent with our survival. Did we not do that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document records once again a bargaining position within the context of the overall negotiations. It's simply a record of where you -- your preferred position at that point in time during the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But is this not a position that makes it possible to establish peace in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Point number 1 is, of course, part of any sensible plan for the opening of the airport, and, indeed, language very similar to that was included in the final agreement which both sides agreed to, and took some time to implement because we couldn't get 48 hours of cease-fire between the signing of the agreement on, I think, the 5th of June and the 24th of June, when I left. Neither party seemed to be able to discipline their forces to impose an agreed cease-fire. But this document here is a bargaining position, Mr. Karadzic. Whether it reflects the final outcome -- what you signed in the end was another document. That's what you agreed to. These are simply bargaining positions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please look at 1D1318. 1D1318.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that the European Community made a lot of effort to keep Izetbegovic on the track at the conference?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which conference are we talking about, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Carrington Conference, the peace conference that was led by Ambassador Cutileiro for Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your first question, then, is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, here we have a telegram. The date is the same. We are discussing the airport issue, and I report to Ambassador Cutileiro that Mr. Izetbegovic responded in the negative to Mr. Carrington's letter about the Bosnia Conference: "He explicitly said in the --" [In English] " ... and that he does not want any conference about the constituent units." [Interpretation] And then I go on to report to him that despite the goodwill we showed in our readiness to open the airport unconditionally: [In English] "We were blackmailed with the lives of JNA families to leave the heavy arms in the barracks "Marsal Tito". This same evening, the Muslim side has started shelling of Serbian residential areas of Sarajevo. "We hope that you can still mediate and bring the Muslim side to the conference." [Interpretation] And so on. Now, General, sir, were you aware of the fact that we were shelled, that the Serb parts of the city were shelled that very night between the 4th and 5th of June?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't surprise me. Many parts of the city were shelled on the night of the 5th of June, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D333, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 65 ter 08496, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in your opinion, who actually started the offensive in the second week of June, on the 7th of June and on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear who started the fighting. I assume you're talking about the fighting around Dobrinja and around the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, around Dobrinja, the airport, in Hadzici, Pazaric, and so on. Do you know that Hadzici is also a part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the geography of that area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the correct document. There has been a mistake, apparently. 08496, 08496. It might be our mistake. Just a moment, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said there seems to be a mistake on his part, so check it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, General, that the city of Sarajevo consisted of 10 municipalities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I were to put it to you that one of the Sarajevo municipalities with a pronounced Serb majority, Ilijas, was shelled on a daily basis and that, proportionately speaking, the largest number of people were killed, civilians and soldiers alike, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many parts of the city were shelled on a daily basis. It could well be that Ilidza was part of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you ever notice in any of the reports that Ilijas was highlighted as a place where many civilians were killed, with a large number of civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no UN presence there or, to my knowledge, international presence there after about the 17th of May until the 24th of June, when I left the city, so we wouldn't have known what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But we published and sent protests, and we published in our media the reports about the suffering of the people in Ilijas. Ilijas begins at a place where you were stopped between Visoko and Sarajevo. That's where Ilijas is, between Visoko and Sarajevo, and it's a purely Serb village, Cekrcici, that had an enormous number of casualties. How come that you did not read the reports in our media about the suffering of the Serbs that were published by the Serb side in their media?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that incident or that series of incidents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please look at 65 ter 11708. Now that's the correct number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is Exhibit P998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, General, please look at number 1. So the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps sent those instructions for further activities to the commander, and the first paragraph reads that: "The enemy commenced a general offensive engaging its forces on the following axes: Zenica-Visoko-Ilijas-Blazuj," and so on. It's probably -- its intentions are to deblock Sarajevo and so on. Do you remember who was blamed for the fighting around Dobrinja from the 7th until the 15th of June?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at my knowledge nobody was blamed. I said that both sides had some tactical interest in securing that area. It was hard to say who initiated the firing. But I said on balance it was my judgement that I thought it was the Serbs, but I don't know that it was ever published or that the Serbs were criticised for that particular tactical action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you that I was under an enormous pressure to put a stop of fighting around Nedzarici and Dobrinja and so on, and you will see now that this had actually been initiated by the other side. In the first passage we can see that the enemy started, and because this is a commander of a Serb unit, it's the Muslims who are the enemy. And then in paragraph 4, he says: "I have decided to mount an active and persistent defence to maintain the lines that have been reached ..." Does this sound like an order to attack?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the same time on the 7th [Realtime transcript read in error "17th"] of June, the Presidency representatives were saying to us that this offensive action had been initiated by the Serbs. Two sides of the same story, Mr. Karadzic, was a very familiar problem for the UN serving in the former Yugoslavia. Unless you actually witnessed it yourself, we have hard evidence, it's impossible to make a determination as to who was responsible for what. Both sides have a different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yet this is not a public document. This is a strictly confidential document. This is what it says there, "The Sarajevo Romanija Corps, Strictly Confidential." And here it says "the extreme defence," and the objective is to maintain security for the aircraft, bringing food and medical supplies to the population living in the broader airport area. So this is not a press release, this was not a report to you. The commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps issues instructions to his subordinate commands as to what they are to do; to defend themselves and to ensure the security of the aircraft. And we will see what the Presidency, itself, was doing on the 17th, on the same day. Can we please look at the last page of this document. It says here in the second paragraph of paragraph 6: "Ill-treatment of unarmed civilian population is strongly prohibited, and prisoners are to be treated in the spirit of the Geneva Conventions. "The use of one combat set of ammunition and half -- 0.5 p/r," I don't know what it means, but this is what he approved for consumption, reminding his units that the civilian population must be treated with respect. And since this document was received, let us look at this document that will tell us what happened on the 17th at the session of the Presidency. They tell you one thing, and yet we can see that the Presidency was doing something completely different. Can we please look at D192. D192, it's a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You didn't ask a question about this document. You just read out the passages and just going into another document. What is your point of reading it? What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is the following: General, do you agree that these are defensive measures that the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps took on the 17th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that he has written that. But whether that happened, I have no way of knowing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Karadzic, is this document dated 7th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7th, for the forthcoming period. The Muslim offensive had already started, and then he actually defines or instructs as to what they have to do in the forthcoming period. This document has already been admitted. And can we then look at D192, the minutes -- the transcript of the tapes of the session of the Croatian Muslim Presidency of the 17th of June that you mentioned a little while ago. Let us look at the reports that Halilovic gives to his Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Halilovic is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 2? I mean in the Serbo-Croatian, because the English page is okay. Mr. Izetbegovic says here: "If the airport does not open, the other side should be to blame, not us. Then we will have a chance to have it opened by force. Surely, that is 90 per cent certain that if he comes back now and says the Serbs will not respect something that is reasonable, which is necessary for the airport to be opened, or fails to accept the conditions generally, in that case there would probably be a resolution which would accomplish that by force." And then further down, he says: "This is what I would like to propose, and then let us see whether we should -- whether we all agree that we should open the airport. Of course, this restricts our army's operations to an extent, but as they say, it's better to have a bird in the hand than in the bush. We'll see what happens."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the logic driving Mr. Izetbegovic here, to accomplish the opening of the airport by force by any means necessary, or a foreign intervention, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see what's written there, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then further down, Ljubic says: "Our hands tied in terms of engaging in penetration." And then Izetbegovic says: "A little bit." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And would that be consistent with what they were telling you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 11th of May -- from the 11th of June, when General MacKenzie arrived in the village in Sarajevo, he and Lieutenant-General Richard Gray conducted the detailed negotiations with both parties for the implementation of the plan. They would be competent to comment on this. I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said that on the 17th of June, the Presidency informed you that the Serbs were causing problems, and here you can see that they are causing problems. So what they're saying here in secret, is it any different from what they are telling you publicly, openly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not having discussions with the Presidency on the 17th of June. I don't know what they're saying. This is the first time I've seen a record of this. The negotiations for the implementation of the airport plan were carried out by General MacKenzie and his staff, not by me. I was deliberately distanced from it because the actual disposition of weapons, which was the military observer interest, was to be on a very restricted basis. Two or three people were to know about it, and I was not one of those to know what the detailed disposition of heavy weapons was to be. This was agreed with General Mladic and also with the Presidency military forces. So I had no knowledge of these negotiations, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A little while ago, you said that on the 17th of June, the Presidency had informed you that the Serbs were causing problems and that you believed them, and yet you do not believe a secret document issued by the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps which was not for public consumption, it was meant for his subordinate commands. You, yourself, mentioned the 17th of June and the Presidency 10 minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was talking about the 7th of June, Mr. Karadzic, not the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 73 of the transcript, I heard you say "the 17th."

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then an error on my part, and my apologies. I thought the conversation then was about the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us check it out. Well, your answer is there on -- it's about the fighting around Nedzarici. Oh, yes, we can see it. Can we locate page 72 and 73? "On the same time on the 17th of June, the Presidency representative were saying to us the same that they had been initiated by the Serbs." Yes, we are coming there. The question appears on line 21, and then your answer starts on line 4 of page 73. Yes, we can stop -- no, no. Yes, we can stop here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's an error on my part. It's the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that on the 15th of June, cease-fire was established, and that the Serb side announced a unilateral cease-fire on the 15th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of cease-fires which were negotiated in the period the 5th of June to the 24th of June, while I was still residing in Sarajevo, and, to my knowledge, none of them held. And on each occasion, each party would blame the other.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us look at page 138 of this document. I don't know the page in e-court, but it says "138" at the bottom, the Serb version. That's the Serb version 138.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, General, General Halilovic reports to his Presidency what they are doing to the Serbs. The whole document is very interesting, and I will go through just two or three short passages with you. In this document, General Halilovic reports that Milinklatska Street was on fire - that's a Serb street - that Trapare Street is on fire. It's a Serb hamlet north east of Dobrinja, up the hill. And here on page 138, he says that: "In the forthcoming stage of the 10 or 15 days --" It's the next page in the English version: "In the forthcoming stage, 10 to 15 days, the Territorial Defence --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting, Your Honour, but Mr. Karadzic said, I think, when he was introducing D192 to the witness, that this was a transcript of the session of the Presidency. In fact, I think this is again just excerpts from this book by Cosic, or Tosic, or somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We haven't the full translation of it, so it is being marked for identification at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think we do have a full translation. No, not a full translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My memory is this has been marked for identification. I think a foundation has been introduced briefly to the witness, but it should have been done in more detail. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, here in the English version, it says "Page 12." Just for your information, the minutes of the Presidency sessions gathered by this man, the fact that he gathered them, it does not change anything. The Prosecution has already established the accuracy of the transcripts. Here, at page 12, he says: "In the subsequent stage, the next 10 to 15 days, the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina will carry out the following activities: "In the region of Sarajevo --" or, rather, "in the co-ordinated action with the TO and HVO, with the active -- will continue the active operations in the Neretva River valley," and so on. And then about Sarajevo, it says: "In the region of Sarajevo, the city of Sarajevo will be defended and action within the city and outside it will be directed at unblocking it in the direction of: Novi Grad, Ilidza, Blazuj, Kiseljak, Centar-Vogosca, Ilijas, Visoko, and in the region of Gorazde unblock the road ..." So you can see what they're planning, and yet there is a cease-fire in force at the time. And then if we move on to the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the general was in contact with the Presidency, and this is what was happening on the 17th of June in the Presidency, while we are under pressure to stop defending ourselves in the Dobrinja, Nedzarici, and so on areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So did you know about this double game on their part?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, on the 17th of June there was fighting all over the city, many different parts. It was -- the operational activity was at a very high tempo. There was a lot of artillery being fired in the city, a lot of infantry fighting. It's difficult to believe they can all be attributed to one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to draw your attention to the next two paragraphs. Izetbegovic asks: "When the engagement of the opposing forces is summed up, how much is that, those that are in the vicinity of Sarajevo and practically surrounding the city ? How many of them are there?" And he goes on to say: "There are about 6.000 in the city of Sarajevo, more specifically those that are surrounding the city." Now, do you see that they're talking about an encirclement, the surrounding of the city, and not the siege of the city? Do you note that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. You'll need to give me time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "There are around 6.000 in the city of Sarajevo, more specifically those that are surrounding the city," or encircling. [Interpretation] Perhaps a better translation would be "encircling the city." [In English] "According to our estimate --" [Interpretation] And in Izetbegovic's question, it says: [In English] "... of Sarajevo and practically surrounding the city." [Interpretation] So it's about men, a realistic assessment of about 80.000 on the territory of B and H: "However, for the city of Sarajevo to completely conquer, much stronger forces are required than those that the Serbs have. Objectively, they cannot accomplish that in the near future unless some radical turning point occurs. However, they will still attempt to accomplish this goal, and the goal is to divide the city of Sarajevo and merge the part from Rajlovac over Stup and Lukavica with Pale. For that goal, objectively they need to have certain forces at their disposal, but in that case their defence would become weaker in other areas, so that is not realistic either ." Now, how many forces did the Muslims have to those 6.000 Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know with any accuracy. I had estimated that there were probably about 15.000. That was my --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned that. You mentioned the figure of about 15.000, and that you said that mostly they were police; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, they were police, and then they were expanded by people being, I guess, recruited into the army. I think the limitation on their numbers, Dr. Karadzic, is not so much the available manpower in the city, but the number of weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm noting the time. It's time to adjourn for today, and then you will have -- you have spent so far about five hours and forty minutes, and you will have about a session -- the first session tomorrow to conclude your cross-examination. Before we adjourn today, now that we'll have the witness KDZ-185, there's a motion pending in respect to the addition of certain documents to the Prosecution's 65 ter list which relates to five documents, one of which is statement and four of them probably photos, so can I hear a response from Defence tomorrow, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, we don't have any objection to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then that's granted, Mr. Tieger. Tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 23rd day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
